opts: Dry January. Proper this time. Write it down. Tell Amy. Make it real.
Just weekdays. Weekends don’t count. That’s still progress.
Hair of the dog. You’re on holiday. January can start Monday.

turns.questionText: If a system knew everything about you — every preference, every fear, every pattern — and used that knowledge to make your life easier, would that feel like care or like captivity?

questionOpts.text: Care. That's literally what a good partner does. What a good doctor does.
Captivity. No matter how comfortable the cage, it's still a cage.
Both. And the fact that it's both is what makes it dangerous.
It depends on whether I asked for it.

paras.t: We all have our good days. Those days when everything seems right with the world. A sense of optimism, of hope. A spring in your step. Filled with the joy of just being alive. Thankful. A warm, fuzzy glow. Whenever I’m in this mood I’m taken back to being a young boy. Five or six. Assembly, first thing in the morning. Sitting cross legged on the wooden floor of my school hall, graced by the rays of the morning sun. All Things Bright and Beautiful. There were other songs sung, but in my memory it’s always this being belted out. The faces from my childhood? I can only bring to mind a few with any clarity. Most are blurry. Ghosts. The names, fewer still. Jason, Simon, Lee, Bruno, James. And of course Vince. Of course Vince. I can’t believe I haven’t told you about him yet. I shall do soon. But that song, the smells (spring flowers vs sour milk) and the feeling. I recall them vividly. That tingly feeling of….what? Happiness? Wonder? Security? Hope? I can’t find the word for it. Maybe there isn’t one? Take never-ending summer holidays, the nostalgia of Stand by Me, my Nan’s rock scones and the cartoon sausage on a fork flying across the screen at the start of Grange Hill. Mix them together. Whatever you get, that’s the word. Tingly is as good as I’ve got. Hopefully you had tingly days too?

Where was I? Ah, good days. This wasn’t one. It was bleak, freezing cold and the boiler had run out of oil. They do that if you forget to check the oil level until the heating stops working. Log fire lit, electric heaters out of the shed. But it’s still freezing. That sent me spiralling, but to be honest I’d woken up in a funk. Actually not a funk, that makes it sound almost whimsical. I’d woken up in a dark sea of despair. Of futility. Of bleakness. Of disgust at the world. And then the oil ran out.

I did not sing All Things Bright and Beautiful. I did not feel tingly. Or fuzzy. Or warm. I felt rage. The song that came into my head was Rape Me. Nirvana. 2 minutes 50 seconds of raw and abrasive brutality. I put it on. I sang along. No, screeched along. It wasn’t cathartic. Well, not in the sense it ‘got it all out my system’. Not a purge. Not a release. A collapse. Literal (I fell to the floor, motionless. The dogs loved it - this is FUN). Emotional. I’d reached my peak.
Rape me.
Vulnerability. Exploitation. Worthlessness. Shame. Desperation. Defeat. Do it.
Rape me again.

To describe it as a low would be to misinterpret the system of measurement. It wasn’t relative, not the other end of the spectrum to inner peace and mindfulness or the opposite of a contented cosy glow. It was a thing in and of itself. Not a void, although I can see why some would liken the feeling to being smothered in nothingness. Not the absence of something. An entity. In fact why am I even trying to find words to describe a feeling. If you know, you know. Me trying to verbalise it with cliched metaphors - abyss, desolation, bottomless pits - is pointless. I’m not a wordsmith. I won’t be able to capture the essence of centuries of romantic poet angst, existential nihilism and the unbearable lightness of being. So I won’t even attempt to. The Dark Night of the Soul. Perhaps The Long Dark Teatime of the Soul, Douglas Adams’ rather more quaint vision of intense, existential boredom, listlessness, and despair, typically occurring on a Sunday afternoon? But on a Monday morning, hungover like a bastard and with the fury dial turned up to 11.
Sorry, I said I’d stop, and I immediately started rambling again. I’ll move on.

I once had a bad trip. Everything came crashing down. Well, melting down, with a fractal overlay. Mel Ting and the Fractal Overlays. Good name for a band, that. Anyway, I’ve brought something up that I don’t want to go into now. Try me on a Sunday afternoon. I mentioned it because it’s the only other experience I’ve had that remotely compares in intensity to my Rape Me Rage. And like all of us I’ve been ‘enriched’ by many intense moments. Loss of my first love, T1 diabetes diagnosis, being told I had cancer. For balance I should mention the good ones. The birth of my children, finding my first love. Finding my true love. The good trips. The 3am ‘one more song’ club nights when the essence of existence was boiled down to a 303 bass-line and a sweaty hug. Looking into someone’s eyes and seeing eternity, that wordless connection. Years of fruitless football-fan toil and disappointment finally making sense as Palace won the FA Cup, those last few minutes of tear-filled, everything-crossed, nerve-wrecking injury time give me shivers every time I replay them in my mind.
See? More good moments than bad. And that’s just a few I’ve rattled off the top of my head.
If I hadn’t seen such riches I could live with being poor

The catalyst for this ‘bad day’ was digital id. Specifically not being ‘able’ to be a company director without One Gov Login. Sounds rather trifling when I put it like that. Bureaucratic. Logical. Private, Secure. But it’s not digital id in and of itself that’s the issue, obviously. It’s all it represents. The tokenisation of our lives. The digitisation of our souls. The control grid. The futility of resistance. Fighting against a tide of managed opposition and manufactured consent. The totalitarian tiptoe inching another yard along the path. Inevitability. What’s that coming over the hill is it a monster? Yes. It’s name? Full spectrum dominance.

I wanted to fight. I wanted everyone to fight. ‘Can’t you see where this is taking us?’ Mass non-compliance. The only way out. ‘Resist Together’ (fuck me, I’ve swallowed a copy of the Behavioural Insights Team for Dummies). ‘OK, but you first’. The Rape Me Rage showed I still had the dog in me. The anguish came from not only knowing that the dog was caged, but that eventually he’d stop barking, curl up semi-contended in a corner. Take a look around.
Actually, it’s not that bad in here. Not bad at all. There’s water, a bed (wonderfully stinky, just how I like it) and a bell. I bet something nice happens if I ring it. Yes! Free bones!

The anguish of knowing that my anger will be ground down to a dull ache. Briefly nullified by a hearty meal and hair-of-the-dog red wine. Going to bed tonight inside a system they can see being built around them. Knowing I should just sleep but powerless to stop myself researching my way out of it. Knowing I’ll be ‘onto something here’ at 3am. Seeing a path. Formulating an action plan. And yet I’ll be impulse buying on Amazon at 8am, Phillips Hue mood-lights automated to ‘morning bliss’ mode, ready for another Starlink-powered day at the coalface.

I’m not the only one. There are many like me, I’m sure. Dogs in cages. No, make that pigs in cages. Content to remain. Not because they’re stupid. Not because they’re weak. Because the checkmate is real.
The 3am researchers, the 8am compliant.
Resistance is a luxury good. Comply or suffer.

choices.label: The soundtrack to your day
opts: Welcome to the Machine
The Show Must Go On
Didn’t We Almost Have It All

paras.t: They have you buy the short and curlies. You can’t vote your way out. Surely you see that by now? Sending sternly-worded letters to MP’s is a humiliation ritual. Signing online petitions is an exercise in futility. Moaning on social media lets off some steam. Which is a major reason why it’s ‘allowed’. A whinge and a scroll into the aether on your algorithmically captured feed might feel satisfying, feel like action, like resistance. But it isn’t.

I’ve been banging on for years about there only being two real options to bring about the changes you want. Either be the change your looking for. Live it. Don’t just think about it, don’t just talk about it. Do it. Positive affirmative action. The issue is that you’ll have to sacrifice an increasing amount to ‘live freely’.

Or fight. Not physically. I’m not talking about storming the bastards with pitch forks. Not until I’ve had a few beers, anyway. I mean mass non-compliance. Unity. Collectively drawing a line and saying ‘this far, no further’. But it doesn’t happen. They know just how far to push us before we break. They’ve got ‘machines and all sorts’ to help them. Insert wink and insanity laugh emojis here. So that’s the impasse we find ourselves at. Complying ourselves into digital cages. Like good little piggies. Oink. Oink.
As the meme goes ‘You are here, paying taxes to paedophiles’.

Flying out to Spain to see my mum and her new puppy (Dash, black spaniel, she’s an absolute dish!) sums up in a nutshell. I can talk a good game. I’ve read more articles than you could shake a stick at about digital id, the surveillance state, technocracy, the panopticon, the algorithmic ghetto, 15 minute cities, SDG 16.9, One Login, interoperability, yada yada. Talk is cheap. I’m a fucking hypocrite and I know it. It’s very easy to say I’m opposed to what looks like (to anyone with half a brain) the formation of a neo-feudalist control grid. But it’s not so easy to stand up and resist.

I know that pretty much every stage of the journey to seeing mum is tracked, analysed, nudged, gated, surveilled and biometrically captured. I’m just giving them my data and my implied consent. Here you go. From the booking of the flights, my naff passwords, VPN-less internet connection being beamed down from Elon’s Skynet, the payment authorisation protocols, the surveillance cameras every 2 metres along the motorway, Google Maps kindly and conveniently helping me avoid the traffic on the way to the airport. The border checks, more cameras, more, more more. And when we land, behold the shiny new EES biometric facial and finger print scanners installed ‘for your safety and convenience’.

Did I give informed consent to any of this? Kind of, read the T’s & C’s, bitch. Do I understand the repercussions of being so liberal with my digital footprint? Yes. Did it stop me getting on a plane to see my mum and Dash? No, it didn’t. Does it stop you? I doubt it. What are we going to do about it? We’re going to look at that Spanish sun and the heated pool in mum’s garden the same way as Cypher looked at that steak.
Ignorance is bliss.
Flight was delayed, weather was pleasant, the Spanish doomscrolling of X remarkably similar to the English version. Adios amigos.

choices.label: When do you draw the line?
opts: I assume someone else will draw it for me.
Soon.
I already have. Look back there, hundreds of lines. They’ve all been crossed.

paras.t: Dev is extraordinary. I've never met anyone else like him. In fact very few people are even quite like him. I met him at school. Christ, nearly forty years ago. He's been an intermittent constant in my life. You can set a clock by his chaotic timekeeping and unreliability. He goes silent for months, occasionally years at a time. He's not what you'd call traditionally responsive to messaging. And I'm not one to push him, if you want to get in touch with him the worst thing you can possibly do is bombard him with texts and calls. ‘Are you OK?’ or ‘Just checking in’ are his Kryptonite. When he does get in touch it's a frenzy. He'll bombard you with months of dense research and be amazed that you don't have an encyclopaedic knowledge of it 24 hours later.
‘Have you read it yet?’
‘No, Dev. You sent it at 2.30am and I've been at work’
‘This is fire though, Simon. Fuck work, drop everything. Read it’

He also has a habit of just ‘finding you’. You won't have seen him for months, last you heard he was in Bangkok or Miami, then he just appears in a pub you hadn't told him you were going to, or knocks on the front door, wanders in and puts the kettle on. No ceremony. No chit chat. Just a hug and straight into a deep dive. It wouldn't surprise me if he'd cut himself a door key and I found him sitting at the kitchen table waiting for me, half a bottle of bourbon down.

But Dev just gets away with it. The rascal's rascal. Nobody has a bad word to say about him, as long as you don't mind being called a cad, a scoundrel, a philanderer, a rogue or a loon. Which he doesn't.

God knows where he gets some of his stuff from. His book recommendations have always been great. He started me on my journey through the sci-fi and dystopian literature landscape. Illuminatus! Trilogy, 1984, Brave New World, Hitchhiker's, Foundation etc. He somehow sent me a pre-release handwritten copy of Ready Player One. It wouldn't surprise me in the least if he'd written it. He'd often just send you a photo of a book. No message. No ‘hi mate’. Just a photo and then dark mode for six months. There are plenty of others, let me think. Off the top of my head, Snowcrash (if you haven't read, read it), Wool, The Road, Children of Time, Cryptonomicon, Daemon, Vurt. Sorry I'm getting carried away, you're not here for book club.

That's just his book recommendations. As I've said he occasionally bombards you with his latest ‘data drop’. 4Chan whistleblowers, alleged intelligence agency leaks and his own mind blowing prose that interweaves fact, fiction, psychedelia and science that goes way over my head. A lot of it quite dark. Yet he somehow manages to offer you an almost empty glass but somehow convinces you it's nearly full. How he retained such positivity I'll never know. Only Forward. (I've unwittingly given you another book recommendation)

Today is extraordinary. He'd actually messaged me to arrange a meeting in a pub, an old London boozer that used to be one of our favourite haunts, and, remarkably, has resisted the urge to gentrify and gastropub itself. Not that it's a conscious entity. In fact, I'll ask Dev, it'll be a good ice breaker. Better than the usual ‘how's the family’. ‘Hi Dev, can a pub have consciousness?’

Four pints in (Timothy Taylor Landlord, with ‘pub buffet’ sides of salted peanuts and pork scratching) and all we've talked about is whether buildings can be conscious. Of course Dev had an angle on this. More than an angle, the entire protractor. It's as if he knew I'd ask him this and he'd been reading up on the subject for weeks. Knowing Dev, he probably did know I'd ask him. Or he just knew this shit anyway. Or both. He started off with Vastu Shastra, an ancient Indian architectural science that sees buildings as fundamentally alive, containing a ‘Vastu Purusha’ (cosmic being) that conducts prana (life force). That led onto Panpsychism, a philosophical position suggesting all matter, including inanimate objects, may have some form of consciousness. Then ‘Smart City’ sensors with AI integration, which might enable ‘dream spaces’ that evolve with their inhabitants, blurring the line between human and machine. We had just started waffling on (to be fair, I was waffling, Dev was lecturing with authority) about substrate-independence, consciousness and complex physical systems, when Alan walked it. I forgot to tell you, Dev had invited Alan along for a beer. He said I'd like him, but nothing more.

Alan was quite remarkable. Part surfer-dude, part gamer-slob, all-American. A big chap, clearly a stoner, amiable, softly spoken, sharp. Imagine The Dude from The Big Lebowski crossed with…well, with no one. Just imagine The Dude. The Dude was wearing Bermuda shorts and Havaianas in English winter. His only concession to the temperature a thin woollen jumper. He apologised for his tardiness (no reason given), bought a round, including 3 pints for himself as he ‘was playing catch up’ and proceeded to neck a pint and a half before he sat down.

I wish I had a recording of the conversation. I'd edit my eight pint pseudo-cringe out and just leave Dev and the Dude. They should do a podcast. Great title. Most of the night (80%) was spent talking about food, mainly burgers. Which cuts of beef to use, cooking method, bun choice, filling, sauce combos. Chunky chips or fries. The perfect burger beer. The best burger joints in the world. Your five-person guest list at your fantasy burger dinner party. The other 20% has been largely sacrificed at the altar of Timmy Taylor. But The Dude was good. Really good. He gave Dev a run for his money. He flipped from burgers (bun intended, I mean pun) to Bounded Systems Theory (no system can model its own source) and back again. He mentioned a ‘prediction engine’ he'd developed. Said he'd ping me something.

I don't think I've ever worried about Dev. I've wondered where the fuck his is and what the hell he's up to. But I've never worried about him. Yet towards the end of the night I thought he looked ruffled. Concerned. Quite out of the blue. Dev never looks ruffled or concerned. He'd been on his phone a bit whilst The Dude was telling me about his engine. Had he read something that freaked him out? Whatever it was, the sudden awkwardness that descended without Dev saying anything stopped The Dude dead in his tracks.
‘You OK mate?’
Dev said he was fine. I knew he wasn't. He had something big, something insane to tell me. Now was not the right time. He'd message me.
And that was that. Apparently he and The Dude had a flight to catch, they got up, we hugged, they left.

The next day I tried to recall the conversations from the night before. Hazy. I remembered snippets, a few nuggets I'd made a mental note of to look into. God knows where Dev and The Dude went. Could be EasyJet to Berlin or Emirates First Class to Abu Dhabi. I don't know which would surprise me more. I was intrigued about what Dev was going to send. It sounded big. But Dev makes everything sound big. I'm sure whatever I get from Alan about his prediction engine will be astonishing. I'll pour myself a White Russian when it arrives and dive in.
The one thing I do remember The Dude saying is this. His parting shot, delivered in an offhand manner, yet somehow it hit.
‘Stop participating in the distractions and create your own reality’

choices.label: The morning after
opts: Google Bounded Systems Theory. What the hell was The Dude on about?
Message Dev. Ask him what's wrong. You've never seen him like that.
Make a White Russian. It's what The Dude would do.

paras.t: A busy week. I won’t bore you with it. Stressful. Work stuff, money, people being people. Well people being arseholes actually. Selfish, unscrupulous bastards. It took me a few days to recover from the night out with Dev and The Dude. Obviously I didn’t hear anything from Dev for four or five days. If it was anyone else it would’ve been a cause for concern, but not Dev. He’d be fine. He was always fine. But I kept getting flashbacks of that look of concern on his face. More than concern. Horror. I was undoubtedly overplaying it. A sober me probably wouldn’t have thought anything of it.

When his message arrived it was somewhat underwhelming. A short document ‘Firmware analysis: UK payment terminal fleet — undocumented OTA push’. Dry, technical. No actual message from Dev, no explanation of what he thought it meant. I’m sure the info about the firmware push was accurate. I don’t doubt that for a second. Dev’s sources are rock solid. What it meant, what he thought it would lead to, wasn’t entirely clear. I searched X, no mention of it. Scanned through several of the hundreds of Telegram groups I had joined over the years but rarely visited. Nothing. Those groups weren’t shy about coming forward with ‘this is the big one’ or ‘they’re gonna bring it all down next week, BE PREPARED’ claims. They’d cried wolf so many times. It seemed to be the sole reason for the existence of some of them, yet nothing on this. Weird.
I pinged Dev a message. ‘What do you think it means?’
I’m still waiting for a reply.
I didn’t think much more of it. I’d been trying to take The Dude’s parting remark to heart.

Stop participating in the distractions and create your own reality. So I made a vow to read an actual book in bed rather than scrolling Substack and X. Small steps. I’ve been reading Freedom, Daniel Suarez, the follow up to the Daemon. Which was bloody amazing. I get through about ten pages per night before I nod off, book still in hand.
‘Are you asleep, Simon?’ Amy asks.

‘No, just thinking’ I fib, smiling. A minute later she’ll have taken the book out of my hands, placed it on my bedside table, bookmark inserted (a dog-eared reminder of a romantic trip to Santorini) and given me a goodnight peck on the cheek. It’s amazing how much better I sleep reading words on paper instead of in blue light.

choices.label: The boy who cried wolf
opts: The wolf is real. You don’t need a boy to tell you it’s coming.
The boy was right. Just early.
Eventually everyone stops listening. That’s when it comes.

paras.t: Talking of The Dude, he sent me a link to his Psychohistory Prediction Engine. The intro sounds so dry. I chuckle to myself. Hard to believe these are the words of the flip-flops in winter, pint-downing stoner I met. I was expecting something more offbeat. More far out.

‘The intellectual trajectory of the last three centuries has been defined by a singular, overriding ambition: the removal of boundaries. We have been told — by scientists, technologists, theologians, and politicians — that limits are temporary. That given enough compute, enough capital, enough time, every wall can be punched through.’
‘This site argues the opposite.’
I’ve been diving in. Mind-blowing. Everyone should be reading it.

choices.label: What’s the reality here
opts: Share it. Right now. With the people that count. Before you forget, before it’s lost in the annals of time.
Bookmark it. You’ll come back to it properly at the weekend. Well, a weekend.
Keep reading. Just one more section. This is fire. Sleep can wait.

paras.t: You've been thinking about the article Dev sent. Silent firmware update pushed to 2 million payment terminals overnight. At first glance, a bit meh. More prepper-shill clickbait. Seen that movie a thousand times. You skim read a few paragraphs and turn in for an early night. Amy is already in bed, reading. A paperback. Old school. Her passion. She gets through one a week minimum. Procedural dramas, romance, that sort of thing. A quick doom-scroll whilst her reading light is still on. A few other accounts are pushing the firmware story too. People you've trusted for years. Proper analysts and researchers. You dig deeper.
3am

Dev was right. This is big. Something's brewing. This isn't a standard firmware update. There's been no announcement. But it appears to be there, lying dormant, waiting for something. For what? They aren't going to flip the switch are they? And when? You've seen a few predictive AI X accounts pointing at Valentine's Day. The symbolism is there, clear as day, in numerous articles. Can't be coincidence? Can it? You eventually nod off just after 3.30am.
Morning

You stir, hot and sweaty. A night of broken sleep. Amy isn't there, you didn't hear her get up. Must be putting the kettle on. 7.44am. 4 hours of poor quality slumber. You pick up the phone, the screen still open on a gematria website you vaguely remember being linked to. 214. Half Man, Half Angel in Hebrew Gematria apparently. You remember 2/14. Valentine's Day.
Here's Amy with a cup of tea and a morning kiss.

choices.label: Morning
opts: Tell Amy. She’ll want to know.
Say nothing. It’s probably nothing. You’ve been here before.
Reply to Dev. Ask him what he actually thinks is going to happen.

paras.t: Amy suggested we try a new walk with the dogs today. A long loop of beautiful Sussex countryside starting and ending at The Bell Inn. She had me at ‘pub’ and she knew it. Only a ten minute drive from our house but somewhere we’d yet to explore. The pub car park was refreshingly busy for dry January.

The skies were clear, the weather brisk, the frost yet to clear from the shaded grass under the trees. I’d wrapped up warm. Woolly hat, thermal socks and underwear, lots of layers and my puffy Fjallräven coat zipped up high to the neck. We walked briskly. The dogs loved it. New smells, new spots for Wilf to mark his territory. Olive got zoomies. And she found a dead rabbit. We found her with it hanging gently from her mouth, no idea what to do with it. Amy took the cutest photo of her.

After twenty minutes or so I started to get hot, my thermals moist from sweat. I took my coat off. Within two to three minutes I was freezing. The hot/cold, coat on/coat off cycle continued until we reached the pub again.
‘Cash preferred, use it or lose it’ a sign outside the pub proudly announces. We smile at one another. Our kind of people. We both know cash is king.
‘Did you bring cash?’
‘No, did you?’
‘No. There’s none in the car either’
We head inside, dogs instinctively head for the roaring log fire.
‘Pint of Best and a Peroni shandy, please. I saw your sign, good to see you keeping cash alive’
‘Yeah, as the sign says, use it or lose it’
‘Annoyingly we left the house without any today, we’ll definitely bring some next time’
‘Thanks, love. £12.40 please’
Tap. Awkward smile.

I join Amy and the dogs by the fire. We make a vow to make sure we always take cash out with us in future. Use it or lose it. There was a day, not sure when it was, that was the last one you made a mental check of money, keys before leaving the house and it became phone, keys.

The beer hits the spot. Half a pint down in a couple of sips. We’re not particularly chatty, tired from the walk. Content just to be, dogs snoozing, fire crackling. The TV is on above the bar. Horse racing, sound turned down at the moment thankfully. I try not to look at it but can’t resist the compulsion to keep glancing up.
‘Eagle Sam’ 9/2 — and the jockey is wearing red and blue. I point it out to Amy. Would’ve stuck twenty quid on if it was the Grand National.
We both notice the TV news ticker —
Defence Secretary: ‘UK faces unprecedented cyber threat from hostile actors’.
They’re really pushing this one. Slowly at first, then all of a sudden.
‘Shall we head?’ asks Amy, breaking a chain of thought that would’ve spiralled. I can feel a 3am deep dive brewing…
We don’t talk much in the car either. Amy unusually quiet. We both know what the other is thinking.

choices.label: Use it or lose it
opts: We’ll bring cash next time. We always say that.
It’s not about cash. It’s about what replaces it.
At least someone’s fighting back.

turns.questionText: what soundtrack does your soul put to this scene?

questionOpts.text: sacral chant
852 Hz frequency
tibetan bowl

paras.t: You've been down this path before. You and Amy packed the garage with dried pasta, tinned tomatoes, cannellini beans and bottled water during 'Covid'. The Great Reset was looming, they were going to pull the rug. War, cyber attack, another mutation that 'targeted the vaccinated'. You ended up taking half of it to the tip as it was past its 'expiry date'. You'd researched what you'd really need if the lights went out and it was more than a few weeks worth of ragu bolognese and linguine. The Prepper sites 'essentials' list would keep Rambo going for years. Weaponry, first aid, water purification systems. The works.

That said, just a few extra supplies wouldn't hurt. Just in case. People you knew, people you trusted were recommending it. A few cases of tinned food. Some Evian. Those 5 litre tins of Cretan extra virgin olive oil on Amazon too. Great value. Packed full of polyphenols.

Some cash too. The lockstep of banks reducing withdrawal limits and the requirement to pre-book appointments (that didn't seem to be available) was odd. People were visibly taking out more cash. Even the normies. But they panic bought bog roll and Marmite, so whatever. You hadn't seen a queue at a cashpoint for years. Not that there are many left. That said, they've been slowly getting rid of cash for years. Plus ça change. The last bundle you withdrew in 2020 was long gone. A pint here, a plumber's bill there. Most of it was paid back into the bank and used to fund some crypto 'investments'. XRP skyrocketed. Then plummeted. The meme coins were a mug's game. You found out the hard way. Still, the gold coins safely hidden in the sock drawer are worth their weight in gold. 2026 edition. Smart, very smart.

choices.label: The garage
opts: Top up the stockpile properly. Prepper list. Do it right this time.
A bit of extra cash, some tins. Don’t go overboard.
Leave it. You’ve done this before. It’ll blow over.

turns.questionText: A government program offers to forgive all your debt in exchange for your biometric data and a digital identity you can never delete. Do you take it?

questionOpts.text: In a heartbeat. Do you have any idea what I'd give to start from zero?
No. If they're offering to buy my identity, it's worth more than my debt.
I'd need to read the terms. All of them. Before I signed anything.
What choice would I have?

turns.questionText: If your phone died permanently right now, what's the first thing you'd feel?

questionOpts.text: Relief.
Panic.
Loss. Like something important just disappeared.
Curiosity. What happens next?

turns.questionText: Is there something about yourself that everyone around you can see but you refuse to acknowledge?

questionOpts.text: Yes. I know what it is. I'm just not ready.
Probably. That's how blind spots work, isn't it?
No. I'm fairly self-aware.
How would I know?

paras.t: Perpetual rain. White skies every day. Not cloudy. White. Not freezing, but certainly big coat weather. Too hot in the woolly hat. Too cold without it. The dogs don't care. The muddier the better. Olive is obsessed with sticks at the moment. Soppy thing. Wilf thinks she's weird. He's old and wise. Log fires every night. Stews. Red wine, but we've been trying to share a bottle rather than one each. The girls are hardly here. Unless they want feeding. Or money. The boys both seem to enjoy university. Costing them an arm and a leg. They better be doing more than enjoying it. I tried to warn them. You'll be saddled with that debt for life. What do I know?

choices.label: Friday evening
opts: Long walk with the dogs. Just you, Olive, Wilf and the mud. Leave the phone at home.
Reply to Dev. You’ve been avoiding it. He sent two more messages today.
Open the Rully Rouge early. Start the Béarnaise. It’s Valentine’s tomorrow. Enjoy something.

turns.questionText: what do you feel?

turns.title: The Last Night at the Fair

paras.t: Valentine’s Day. We’re staying in. Always have done. Two courses in the local gastropub — 200 quid better spent elsewhere — a couple of pints. A bottle of red, probably two. I won’t be able to resist the cheeseboard. Drive there, taxi back, pick the car up in the morning. Rigmarole.

Anyway I’m a decent cook. Amy is too. We’re a good team. I’m meat and sauces. She’s veg and presentation. We rarely argue. We don’t get in each other’s way. We giggle. We’re silly together. Keeps us young and vibrant.

The flat iron from our local butcher is insanely good. The depth of flavour of a ribeye with the melting tenderness of a fillet. I’ll cook it on the griddle, charred on the outside, rare in the middle. Maybe veering towards medium rare to keep my darling happy. Compromise. It’ll rest on a huge slab of oak chopping board. Adds a rugged, rustic charm as a table centrepiece. A bugger to wash up though. Tomorrow morning’s problem. Triple cooked duck fat chips. Steamed spinach. Tomatoes roasted in olive oil with copious amounts of Maldon and black pepper. Just normal peppercorns freshly ground from our tall artisan-made mill. We used to spend three times as much on Tellicherry. Couldn’t taste the difference. I’ll start making the Béarnaise too early. It will be perfect. Simmering on a low heat waiting for its chip dipping, meat slathering fate. Buttery, glossy, thick, speckled with fresh tarragon and sharp with white wine vinegar. I’ll nurse it, stirring slowly. I won’t take my eye off it. Until I do. Then it’ll split. I’ll remain calm, seething inside. Unless I’ve been on the gin. Doesn’t suit me. Whoever called it Mother’s ruin was on the money. Anyway I’ll thicken it up with another egg yolk or an ice cube. It’ll be fine.

It all went to plan. Even the Béarnaise split. The wine was delightful. Our ‘treat’ wine. Rully Rouge Premier Cru Clos du Chapitre, Jaeger-Defaix. God it’s good. Silky, pure, plenty of berry fruit, but with some guts too. And yes, we’ve just opened the third bottle. Kitchen disco in full swing. Started off chilled. A bit of background jazz. Flowed seamlessly into some Café del Mar. The early José Padilla stuff of course. I’d planned to get the vinyl out tonight. I’m an avid collector. Well I was. I can’t remember the last time I bought an album. I tell everyone how digital music is inferior to analogue vinyl LPs. The artwork. The warm and natural sound. A more engaging listening experience. Superior dynamic range. Full-album appreciation. Stories told over multiple tracks. Tactile. Real.
I can’t remember the last time I put one on the turntable.

So here we are sitting on stools by the kitchen island. We’ve been playing ‘song tag’ — Amy chooses first, then me, then back to Amy. Spotify Premium played on Sonos Play 5. Not cutting edge, but sounds good to me. We’re now at the dancey stage of proceedings. She chose Higher States of Consciousness. I replied with Smack My Bitch Up. Love The Prodigy. And it is Valentine’s Day! We’re now listening to Insomnia. Which means it’ll soon be bedtime. I’ve got the Age of Love lined up next. Jam and Spoon Watch Out For Stella Mix, of course. Remember we played together….

Starlink has been a bit hit and miss today, but most of these songs are all saved in our Spotify Library. This ain’t our first rodeo. Age of Love is queued to come on next. The thought of those hypnotic, otherworldly beats at the start make my spine tingle. It’s taking its time to play, what’s happening? Wheel of death on the phone. Weird. I’m sure it was in a playlist in the Library. Sod it. I’ll get it out on vinyl. Bloody technology. It’ll sound better too. I rummage through the collection, it’s in here somewhere. I dumped the piles of vinyl in random order on the shelf when we moved house 3 years ago (wait 4, no 5 years ago. Where did all the time go?) and promised myself to reorganise it into its former orderly glory. Never happened. Anyway, I found it. Eventually. I took it out of its sleeve, a million memories of top-off, wide-eyed, sweaty nights released with it. Onto the turntable it goes. The familiar plop as the spindle emerges through the hole. I hear my needle hit the groove (mental note, Stone Roses next).

Age of Love hits its angelic voices crescendo. I’m dancing, eyes closed. My body in 2027. My mind in 1995. The dying years of The Before Times. Not that we knew it then. Tears well up in my eyes. Time’s tide has smothered me. My nostalgia spiral has started. I can’t help but think of her.
Amy shows me her phone. She can’t send a WhatsApp. She tries a text. Not sending. ‘Try calling me’. She clicks on ‘Simon’. Nope. Nothing. Weird. I check my emails. Nothing received since just past 9.
Probably the cyber attack we’ve been promised, I jest as I load up She Bangs The Drums.
I smile at Amy. She’s my Rock. My Love. My Everything.

How could it ever come to pass
She’ll be the first, she’ll be the last
To describe the way I feel
The way I feel

choices.label: Late night
opts: Keep fiddling with your phone.
Cuddle Amy and stroke her hair reassuringly.
Crash out.

paras.t:
Creaky noises make my skin creep
I need to get some sleep….
I can't get no sleep
Where are you? In bed, check.
How do you feel? Neck's sore. Note to self. I need new pillows. Mouth is dry. Reach for water. The glass is full. Big glug.

What time is it? Actually what day is it? Feels early and maybe a Sunday. Reach for phone. It's there, usual spot on the bedside table. You remembered to charge it before crashing out. First Brownie point of the day.
6.16am. Early doors.

I should check the girls' location. Did they get back to Sophie's after the party. Obviously Amy will have checked, but I should do my due diligence too. I turn to look at Amy. Deep sleep still. Away with the fairies, mumbling something about leaks. Or maybe it's leeks? I'll ask her when she wakes up. Doubt she'll remember it. She'll find it funny though. I look forward to seeing that smile.
Go to 'Find my' App. Emilia - Last seen 7 hours ago. Swipe down to update. No change. Click on Chloe - the same, 7 hours ago.
You remember the service being shit last night. All three curves of full signal Wi-Fi reassurance.
See if the internet is working. BBC propaganda check first.
Nothing. Try something else…Crystal Palace blog…Nothing.
Fuck's sake.
Is Starlink aligned? In fact, I'll just reboot the hub first. And put the kettle on.
ARC?
Hub rebooted. Kettle on. Still no service.
X…just nothing. Insta….also nothing.
Weird.
Barclays App. 'Closed for routine maintenance'

Kettle's boiled. 2 mugs. Earl Grey and 1 spoon of sugar. Must be Demerara. Builders for me. And I'm sweet enough already. Back to the bedroom. The gentle clunk of mug on bedside table causes Amy to stir. Well, not gentle as much. Honed to perfection over the years to be just loud enough to wake her with the knowledge that her tea hero has come to the rescue, not too loud as to be an annoyingly obvious 'wake up and play'.
'Morning'
'Morning, darling. Cup of tea on the side for you.'
'I know. My hero. I'll make the difficult second cup.'
(It never gets old)
'Bloody internet is still down'
'Is it? Are the girls OK?'
'Don't know. Everything is down'
She jolts upright, reaching for the phone.
'You're right. Last seen 7 hours ago. Have you tried calling?'
I hadn't.
'No, I didn't want to wake them' I replied, half truthfully. 'They'll be fine'
'What's this, Simon?'
I got a Simon, something is amiss. She points at a small blue swirly logo under the battery percentage bar. Hers was 100%.
“An app called ARC. That’s weird, I don’t remember installing that.”
I look at my phone. Same logo, same ARC app. I click on it. It does nothing.

choices.label: ARC
opts: An app called ARC that does nothing. Weird.

paras.t: Amy left a half-drunk cup of tea on the kitchen worktop. It was highly unusual for her to start her day without kickstarting herself with at least three cups, often accompanied by a few rounds of Marmite on toast.

She was worried about the girls. She was always worried about the girls. They'd be fine, they were at Sophie's, they were safe, the internet would be back up and running soon. It'd be much ado about nothing as it always is. Without all the 'cyber attack' warnings and 'increased threat levels' we'd have simply thought the internet was down. The (difficult) second and (straightforward if I was making it) third cups of tea would've been made and drunk.

But this smacked of being an 'event' - a 'happening'. Concocted. Implemented. Controlled. The 'Big Story' that the media would latch onto. 'If it's in the news it's likely a ruse'. Stir up some panic, seed a bit of fear, ensure the algo-boosted X accounts throw in a splattering of 'this is the big one' in. BBC Verify, the arbiter of truth, setting everyone straight. Some political bluster in the days to follow - 'what we should do to ensure this doesn't happen again?' (Answer - more robust verification processes, more control, more surveillance. Same as always. They'd definitely use the word 'robust', I'd stake my mortgage on it. And they'd definitely give more millions to Palantir or Oracle to guarantee the increased robustness).

Anyway, Amy didn't finish her first cup as she panic-left the house just after 6am, un-showered and in a tizz, to go and check on the girls. I'd said they'd still be asleep. Probably for another 5 hours. If they've even gone to bed yet. We'd let them stay with Sophie on a Sunday night as they had a day off college today. Amy rushed out. 'Love you, I'll be back soon'. I put the kettle on to make myself a particularly challenging second cup and absentmindedly picked up my phone for the morning email/X/BBC headline check.

Nothing.

Darkness. Despite knowing there'd be nothing it still surprised me. The nimble-fingered unconscious info-sweep and instant dopamine hit is so engrained. I used to wake up and have a spliff when I was at University. My first contact with the world a perusal of The Sun (I know, I was young and liked there, sport section) on the tube to central London. Nowadays the psyops start before I've even had a piss.

6.07am. The clock is the only thing that's working on my phone. Well, that and the torch. All the apps open but state various versions of 'service unavailable' I tried the Mac and the iPad too. Nothing. Reset the router a few more times. Starlink app opens OK — claims 'Starlink is aligned' — but also tells me it's 'Offline' and the router is 'unreachable'. Annoying. I had set aside the morning for sending out invoices to market traders, but this relied on Quickbooks Online, which was just hanging. Not even a courtesy 'we'll be back online soon'.

At least the power was on. Cup of tea number three and a couple of slices of toast. Hungry Guest 'chewy brown'. Quite possibly the best loaf known to man. Buttered when hot, melting and collecting in the sourdough pools. A carby treat for my hangover. Extra insulin needed, 12 units should do it. Hardly scientific but an educated guess after years of carb-counting, trail and error.

Kate knocked. She was supposed to be on a video call with a client. Just checking if our internet was still down too. Asked her in for a tea but she wanted to go back next-door and try and get the call to work.

I checked What's App again. Lots of grey single ticks. No one was receiving my messages. I had one message from Vince. 1.01am. He'd obviously had issues too but seemingly sorted in London now. Reassuring.

I sat in the beaten up leather armchair in the hallway. Slurping, crunching, chewing. No phone. Just me, my thoughts, a view of the plants in the courtyard outside the front door. The olive tree had wintered well. The magnolia looking as if it would soon blossom into its early Spring glory. The dogs settled at my feet. Peace. I could get used to this.

I was just starting to nod off when I heard the sound of a key trying to fit into the front door lock. George was back. What the hell was he doing back just after 6 in the morning? Looked even more hungover than I felt. He'd been for a Valentine's booze at the local with his mates and crashed on Thomas's sofa. Couldn't sleep, so decided to head home. Undoubtedly over the limit still. It was only a short drive though, country lanes.

We confirmed to one another that the internet was fucked. (His words. Actually mine too, come to think of it.) He'd tried to call Amy but was getting either nothing, straight-to-voicemail or endless ringing with no answer.

'Have you tried the TV' he asked. I hadn't thought of that. We turned it on. Just a black screen. Of course it is, we'd watched TV over the internet via a Amazon Fire TV Box for years. 'Does this thing even have 'normal' TV?' I asked George. He had no idea. He thought we did watch normal TV. 'Cup of tea, Georgie?' 'No thanks, I'm knackered. See you on the other side.' He slunk off to his room.

turns.title: I am the God of Hellfire

paras.t: What the hell is that? The most God-awful noise. Ear piercing. The dogs barked in unison. Wilf, hackles up, deep and manly followed by a growl. Olive, bemused look on her face, higher pitched and more incessant.
George burst back into the hallway, the door somehow staying on its hinges.
'What the…?'
He showed me his phone. The source of the sound identified. The klaxon I assumed was only ever for Emergency Alert tests and scaremongering.
UK GOVERNMENT EMERGENCY ALERT

I skim read it in disbelief. Major cyber incident…UK financial and digital infrastructure…Emergency services…card and electronic banking payments have been suspended…and then at the bottom… from the same people who brought you The Plandemic…
STAY HOME. STAY CALM.

paras.t: She said nothing. She played Northern Sky by Nick Drake. We hugged. We cried. We left for the Community Recovery Hub.

I never felt magic crazy as this
I never saw moons, knew the meaning of the sea
I never held emotion in the palm of my hand
Or felt sweet breezes in the top of a tree
But now you're here
Brighten my northern sky
Mid Morning
It was the discussion on everyone's lips. But ask the majority if they were registering you'd get a bemused look. What do you mean if?

On the face of it who could argue? Debts erased, £1000 per month (well 1000 Brits, same same), food hampers. And hampers they were. A far cry from ration books and make-do-and-mend. Fresh, healthy, tailored to your dietary requirements, customisable, delivered to your door. And free. And for what, registering on a 'new App'.
They simply couldn't be made to see the downside. Or they refused to acknowledge it. As Cypher said, 'ignorance is bliss'.
Some could see it, of course. We'd been on the protests. I'd say there were more there than there were for the Lockdown marches.
Amy could see it. Of course she could. Or perhaps she felt it — that would be more accurate. Some things she simply understood.
Very female. Very Amy. Not knowledge. Intuition.
I'd put in the hard yards. Hour upon hour of research and 'deep dives'. Over a decade's worth. I had a file on them and they sure as hell had a file on me. They had a file on everyone.
Why are they doing this? She simply couldn't comprehend evil. But she knew there was a 'they'.

She'd be in floods of tears if she saw a dead deer on the road. It's not fair that this beautiful creature must die. I would be upset, but that was the way of the world. I didn't have her empathy. Not many did.
This however, this was beyond her comprehension. I responded with rage. She responded with sadness. Infinite sadness.
I didn't know what to say, what to do. I knew what was going on. Well I thought I did. I used to think I did. I was having my doubts. What if this is just progress, what if it's just better.
Karma police, arrest this man

I'd bombarded her, everyone and anyone who'd listen, with my 'research'. Sent links to essays by investigative journalists, punchy truth movement YouTube videos. Shown them scientific papers. I had a bulging digital file of them. I had half-read paperbacks exposing the whole nine yards. I'd talked about neo-feudalism, transhumanism, satanism, spiritual warfare, prophecy of the Third Temple, eschatology, eugenics. The list goes on. And on. I'd even jokingly prepared a conspiracy-nutter style presentation on a whiteboard, joining the dots with string. Some listened. Some shrugged. Some stared blankly. Some laughed. Many asked who are 'they'?

I'd tell all my friends, but they'd never believe me
They'd think that I'd finally lost it completely

Yet here I was. Already AIDA registered. Clean, easy, quick. 1000 Brits in my wallet. Soon to be several thousand more once we've presented our statements at the 'Community Recovery Hub'. You couldn't make this shit up. But someone did. They did. Oh, plus the house. In our name. No mortgage.
Soon they'll call our names and ask 'papers, please?'

What else can I be?
All apologies

article.title: PS26/4: Authenticated Residential Computing (ARC) — Implementation Notice
article.body:
The Financial Conduct Authority confirms that the ARC authentication framework will be integrated across all UK-regulated payment infrastructure by 30 September 2026, as outlined in Consultation Paper CP25/12.

ARC provides a unified device-level authentication layer across payment terminals, banking applications, and regulated financial services platforms. It standardises identity verification at the hardware level, replacing the current patchwork of vendor-specific authentication protocols.

All acquirers (Worldpay, Barclaycard, Global Payments, etc.) are required to push ARC integration to merchant terminal fleets via scheduled firmware updates. ARC operates below the application layer and requires no merchant action or configuration. End users will not experience any change to transaction workflows.

ARC has been developed in coordination with the Bank of England, the Payment Systems Regulator, and the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub (Basel). Compliance is mandatory for all FCA-regulated payment service providers.

Further technical documentation: fca.org.uk/arc-implementation

article.title: What’s Sitting Inside Two Million Payment Terminals
article.body:
I’ve spent the last 72 hours examining the firmware push that a document circulating on Signal and Telegram describes in detail. I’m not going to link to that document. If you’ve seen it, you know what I’m referring to. If you haven’t, this post will make the case independently.

On the night of 28–29 January, approximately 2.1 million Ingenico and Verifone payment terminals across the UK received an over-the-air firmware update. This is not disputed. What the vendors have declined to confirm is who authorised it, and what the payload contains.

I’ve analysed the firmware hash. It matches the document. Here is what’s inside.

The container

The payload installs a dormant service container. It does not activate. It does not interfere with existing payment processing. It sits alongside the terminal’s standard operating software and waits.

The container has three capabilities that no UK payment terminal has ever required:

First: local biometric template storage. The terminal can now store and match fingerprint and vein-pattern data. No current UK payment workflow involves biometrics at the point of sale. Contactless, chip-and-PIN, mobile wallet — none of these require your fingerprint. So why does the terminal now have space for it?

Second: NFC write access. Current terminals read NFC — they receive data from your phone or card. The updated terminals can also write to NFC devices. They can push data to your phone. Think about what that means. The payment terminal becomes a two-way channel.

Third: an encrypted callback to a routing address that resolves not to Worldpay, not to Barclaycard, not to Global Payments — but to infrastructure operated by the Bank for International Settlements in Basel.

The ARC connection

The container hooks directly into ARC — the Authentication and Registration Core that was rolled out across UK payment infrastructure last autumn. ARC was described as a device-level identity verification framework. It is now clear that ARC is the authentication layer for whatever this new capability is.

The same ARC framework is now running in UK airports under the Seamless Border Programme. The same biometric template format. The same data architecture. A fingerprint scanned at Gatwick and a fingerprint scanned at a card terminal in Tesco would be verified by the same system.

The time-lock

The activation window is encrypted. The date is not disclosed in the firmware. But the deployment was simultaneous — every terminal updated on the same night — and the activation mechanism is designed to trigger every terminal at the same moment. Whatever this is designed to do, it is designed to do it everywhere at once, on a date the deployers have chosen not to reveal.

What this means

I want to be careful here. I am not a conspiracy theorist. I am a payment systems analyst with fifteen years in the industry. I have worked for two of the three acquirer networks involved in this deployment.

What I am looking at is infrastructure for a new payment system — biometric, two-way, centrally controlled, routed through the BIS — that has been pre-positioned inside two million existing terminals without merchant knowledge, without vendor acknowledgement, and without regulatory disclosure.

It is not active. It is waiting.

I don’t know what it’s waiting for.

items.text: The Seamless Border Isn’t About Borders

article.title: The Seamless Border Isn’t About Borders
article.body:
The Home Office’s Seamless Border Programme went live this week at all 32 UK commercial airports. BBC Travel ran a helpful explainer about queue times. Nobody mentioned what the system is actually built on.

The facial recognition layer runs on ARC — the same Authentication and Registration Core that was quietly rolled out across UK payment terminals last autumn. The same framework. The same biometric template format. The same data architecture. Your face at the airport gate is verified by the same system that will verify your face at a card terminal.

This is called interoperability. It means one identity framework serving multiple functions — travel, payment, age verification, access control. Each function justified independently. Together they constitute a single digital identity infrastructure with no opt-out.

The 340 “secondary screening” referrals at Gatwick in week one are worth paying attention to. Under the old system, referrals were based on document irregularities — expired passports, damaged chips. Under the new system, referrals are generated by algorithmic confidence scores. The threshold is set by the Home Office. It is not published. It can be adjusted remotely.

What does a low confidence score correlate with? The Home Office won’t say. Independent researchers analysing similar systems in the EU have documented consistent bias against darker skin tones, non-Western facial structures, and — notably — individuals with sparse or irregular digital footprints. If you don’t have much data in the system, the system doesn’t recognise you well. The less integrated you are, the more friction you experience.

This is the algorithm ghetto. Not a physical barrier. A confidence score.

The programme is described as “voluntary for now” for land crossings and domestic rail. The March deadline for airlines to remove manual checks suggests the window for that language is short.

Nobody is being forced through the gate. The gate is simply the only gate that works.

article.title: Beyond chatbots: what 2027 will really mean for AI
article.body:
If 2024 was the year AI learned to talk, 2025 the year it learned to see, and 2026 the year it learned to listen, 2027 is shaping up to be the year it learns to do.

The large language models that powered the first wave of consumer AI — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini — were built on the transformer architecture, a neural network design introduced in 2017 that excels at modelling sequences using “attention” to decide what matters. It was astonishingly effective for text, and increasingly for images, audio and code.

But the next wave won’t be defined by bigger models. It will be defined by different ones.

Multimodal-native systems are arriving that reason across text, images, audio and video as first-class inputs — not bolt-ons stitched together in a pipeline. Google’s latest research demos show models that can watch a live video feed and answer questions about what’s happening in real time. The implications for accessibility, education and healthcare are significant. So are the implications for surveillance, though few in the industry are saying that out loud.

Agent-style systems — AI that doesn’t just generate text but takes actions — are moving from demo to deployment. Today this looks like early-stage tool use and function calling: book a restaurant, file an expense, draft and send an email. By late 2027, industry insiders expect goal-driven orchestration: give the AI an objective and let it figure out the steps. Microsoft’s AutoGen framework and Anthropic’s tool-use protocols are the early scaffolding.

Retrieval-augmented generation is quietly solving the hallucination problem. Instead of asking a model to remember everything, you fetch relevant documents at query time and feed them in. The model reasons over verified sources rather than its own training data. For enterprise, government and healthcare — where accuracy is non-negotiable — this is the architecture that unlocks adoption.

Smaller, specialised models running on-device are the sleeper story. Apple’s on-device intelligence, Qualcomm’s NPU chips, and a wave of edge-deployed models mean your phone, your watch, your car, your fridge will run their own AI locally. No cloud round-trip. No latency. No data leaving the device — in theory.

And then there’s the category nobody quite knows how to name: hybrid neuro-symbolic systems that mix learned pattern recognition with explicit rules and structured reasoning. Less hallucination. More auditability. Potentially more aligned with regulatory frameworks like UK GDPR and the EU AI Act. The AI Safety Institute has flagged these as “the most promising path to trustworthy AI in public services.”

For UK organisations, the practical implications are immediate. Don’t build everything around a single vendor or model — use abstraction layers that let you swap components as the landscape shifts. Design for audit now, not later. And invest in durable skills: data quality, evaluation, model governance. These outlast any single architecture.

The companies that will define 2027 aren’t necessarily the ones that defined 2024. The transformer was the internal combustion engine of AI. What comes next might be the electric motor: quieter, cleaner, and everywhere before you notice.

items.text: SciTechDaily — From home robots to AR lenses: 2027–2028

article.title: From home robots to AR lenses: the technology arriving in 2027–2028
article.body:
Every year, the predictions get bolder. Every year, some of them come true. Here’s what’s actually shipping — or credibly close to shipping — in the next eighteen months.

Home robots: this time it’s real

Tesla’s Optimus Gen 3 enters limited home deployment in Q2 2027. Priced at $18,000 — roughly the cost of a mid-range car — it’s designed for household tasks: laundry folding, dish loading, basic cooking prep, elderly care assistance. Early reviews from the US pilot programme describe it as “eerily competent at boring things.”

Boston Dynamics’ Stretch platform, originally industrial, now has a consumer variant for warehouse-style home organisation. Samsung’s Ballie — delayed twice — finally ships with a full home-management suite: it vacuums, monitors energy usage, and acts as a roving security camera that follows you from room to room. Whether that’s reassuring or unsettling depends on your perspective.

The UK market is expected to see first shipments by Christmas 2027. Analysts predict 400,000 home robots in British households by 2029.

AR lenses: the Metaverse v2.0

The first Metaverse push failed because it asked people to strap a headset to their face and stand in a cartoon. The second attempt is subtler.

Meta’s Orion glasses — true augmented reality in a form factor that looks like regular spectacles — enter developer preview in March 2027. Apple’s Vision Pro 2 drops the ski-goggle aesthetic for something closer to wraparound sunglasses. Both overlay digital information on the physical world: navigation arrows on pavements, recipe steps floating above your chopping board, translated subtitles hovering beneath a foreign speaker’s face.

But the real shift is contact lenses. Mojo Vision’s smart lens — delayed from 2025 — is now in clinical trials with an expected consumer launch in late 2028. A display built into a contact lens. Information projected directly onto your retina. No device visible to anyone else.

The implications for work, education and social interaction are vast. The implications for privacy are terrifying. If everyone around you could be recording, reading contextual data about you, or receiving AI-generated prompts about how to interact with you — and you’d never know — the social contract changes fundamentally.

Nobody in the industry talks about that. They talk about “seamless integration” and “ambient computing.”

Wearable health monitoring

The NHS’s wrist-worn wellness monitor pilot — 50,000 volunteers, launched in October — is generating data that Public Health England describes as “transformative.” Continuous heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep quality, and stress indicators streamed to a centralised health dashboard.

The pilot is voluntary. The data is anonymised. The results are promising: early detection of atrial fibrillation, flu-like illness flagged 48 hours before symptoms, and a 23% reduction in unnecessary GP visits among participants.

The government has signalled that a nationwide rollout is “under active consideration” for 2028. Integration with the NHS App is already in development. The device would be free — funded by projected savings to the health service.

A free health monitor from the government that streams your biometrics to a central database. The fact that this is framed as a gift rather than surveillance tells you everything about where the Overton window has moved.

Smart home convergence

Matter — the interoperability standard backed by Apple, Google, Amazon and Samsung — reaches critical mass in 2027. For the first time, every smart device in your home speaks the same protocol. Your heating, lighting, locks, cameras, appliances and entertainment system operate as a single mesh, managed by a conversational AI assistant.

The assistant is the brain. The home is the body. The data is the nervous system.

Analysts at McKinsey estimate that by 2028, the average UK smart home will generate 1.4 terabytes of behavioural data per year — equivalent to monitoring every member of the household 24 hours a day. This data is, in theory, private. In practice, it flows through cloud services operated by three or four companies, under terms of service that most users have never read.

“The smart home isn’t smart,” says Professor Carissa Véliz, author of Privacy is Power. “It’s obedient. And it’s not obedient to you.”

What it all adds up to

Individually, each of these technologies solves a genuine problem. Home robots save time. AR enhances experience. Health monitors save lives. Smart homes save energy. The question nobody is asking loudly enough: what happens when they’re all connected, all feeding data to the same platforms, and all managed by the same AI layer?

The answer, probably, is that life gets measurably better for most people. And measurably more transparent to whoever controls the infrastructure.

That’s the trade-off of 2027. It’s the same trade-off as every year. Just more of it.

article.title: Why millions are switching to conversational AI assistants — and what it means for the future of search
article.body:
A new generation of AI assistants is rewriting the rules of how people interact with technology — and the speed of adoption has taken even their creators by surprise.

In the past six months, conversational AI platforms have moved from novelty to necessity for millions of users worldwide. Unlike the chatbots of two years ago — stilted, formulaic, prone to confident errors — the latest models feel different. Users describe them as “intuitive,” “warm,” and “almost unsettlingly helpful.”

The shift is being driven by a cluster of platforms that emerged in late 2026, most notably Aria (backed by a European research consortium), alongside updated offerings from the major US tech companies. What sets this generation apart is personalisation. The assistants don’t just answer questions — they learn preferences, anticipate needs, and adapt their tone to the individual user.

“It’s like talking to someone who actually knows me,” said one user in a BBC-commissioned survey. “I use it for meal planning, homework help, appointment booking. I don’t Google things anymore.”

Adoption figures are striking. Aria alone has registered 140 million active users since its September launch, with particularly strong uptake in the UK, EU, and Commonwealth nations. A University of Oxford study found that 68% of users aged 16–34 now use a conversational AI assistant daily — up from 12% eighteen months ago.

The technology is built on large language models, but the new platforms integrate real-time data feeds, health monitoring APIs, and — controversially — optional biometric voice authentication, allowing the assistant to verify identity by voice alone.

Privacy campaigners have flagged concerns about the volume of personal data these systems process. The AI Safety Institute has called for “urgent regulatory clarity” on data retention and consent frameworks.

But for most users, the experience is simply too good to resist. Dr Elena Torres, a digital anthropologist at UCL, describes the dynamic as “convenience gravity” — the pull of a system that makes every interaction fractionally easier, until opting out feels like opting out of modern life itself.

“Nobody is being forced to use these tools,” Dr Torres said. “That’s precisely what makes them so effective. The best adoption is voluntary adoption.”

Aria’s European backers include the Digital Innovation Hub, a consortium with funding from the European Commission, the Bank for International Settlements’ Innovation Hub, and several national central banks. The consortium has positioned Aria as an “open, ethical alternative” to US-dominated AI platforms.

The UK government announced last week that its One Login digital identity programme will integrate conversational AI assistance from April, allowing citizens to complete tax returns, benefit applications, and passport renewals through natural conversation rather than form-filling.

Analysts predict that within two years, conversational AI will be the primary interface between citizens and government services in most developed nations.

“We’re not building a product,” said an Aria spokesperson. “We’re building a relationship.”

article.title: The Deployment Pattern Nobody Is Talking About
article.body:
I’ve been tracking UK military deployments for eleven years. What’s happening right now is not routine.

The MOD’s “Defence Readiness Programme” exercises follow a predictable annual cycle. Spring: Salisbury Plain and Scotland. Autumn: East Anglia (usually coinciding with NATO commitments). Winter is typically maintenance cycle — reduced activity, not expanded.

Here is what has actually happened since October:

October 2026: RAF Wyton — described as “routine exercise.” Wyton is home to the Joint Forces Intelligence Group. It is not an exercise facility. It is an intelligence hub. You don’t run readiness exercises at an intelligence base. You run intelligence operations.

November–December 2026: Deployments across East Anglia and the Midlands. Light vehicles, signals equipment, mobile communications arrays. Not combat units. Logistics and communications.

January 2027: Expansion to southern England. Hampshire, West Sussex, Surrey. Thirty-vehicle convoys on the A272. Again: logistics. Mobile generators. Fuel bowsers. Field hospitals spotted near Bordon.

The pattern is not combat positioning. It is continuity-of-government positioning. These are the units you deploy when you expect civilian infrastructure to fail and need military logistics to fill the gap. Field hospitals. Mobile comms. Fuel distribution. Food supply chain support.

Three details worth noting:

First, the deployment arc is tightening toward London. October: Cambridgeshire. December: Midlands. January: the Home Counties. If you were establishing a logistics perimeter around the capital, this is what it would look like.

Second, the timing overlaps almost exactly with the NCSC’s escalation from “normal” to “heightened” cyber threat level. The military began positioning before the threat level was raised. Either they had advance warning, or the threat level was raised to provide cover for positioning that was already underway.

Third, none of this has been discussed in Parliament. The Defence Secretary’s statement on Wednesday referenced “hostile state actors” and “unprecedented cyber threats.” He did not mention the domestic military deployments. MPs did not ask.

I’m not drawing conclusions. I’m drawing a map. The map shows military logistics assets being pre-positioned across southern England in a pattern consistent with preparing for a major disruption to civilian infrastructure.

items.text: PM’s Address to the Nation — 15 February 2027

article.title: PM’s Address to the Nation — 15 February 2027
article.date: 15 February 2027 — 6:00pm GMT — BBC Television, Radio and ARC Emergency
article.body:
Good evening.

Yesterday, on Valentine’s Day, a little before midnight, a coordinated cyber attack struck the financial and digital infrastructure of the United Kingdom and twenty-two other nations. This has caused significant disruption to civilian systems in our nation and around the globe.

Here is what we know. I will not minimise it. The attack targeted the core transaction and record-keeping systems that underpin our banking, our public services, and much of our daily communication. Our security and intelligence services, working in close coordination with international partners, are engaged in a comprehensive response. I chaired COBRA at six o’clock this morning and have been in continuous session since.

Here is what I want you to understand. The damage is being assessed. The infrastructure is damaged, not destroyed. We are working — with every resource available to us — to restore normal service. Our current assessment is that this will take days, not weeks.

The power grid is stable and being actively managed. Water and gas supplies are unaffected.

Currently we are unable to access our bank accounts. Shops and businesses are unable to process our card payments. For this reason, for the next 36 hours retail, businesses and offices will be closed. A detailed plan for the opening of essential retail, including supermarkets, will be issued shortly.

Schools were closed today and will remain closed for the remainder of the week. Hospitals remain open for emergencies only; all routine and non-urgent care has been postponed, also for the remainder of the week. All public transport services are suspended for the same period of time.

Our emergency services are operational. Our military and police forces will be visible, on the streets, to ensure the safety of every one of us.

The emergency communications platform on your phones — many of you will have already received alerts through it — is functioning as designed. It will continue to be your most reliable source of verified information in the coming days.

Part of this emergency communication system is ARC. You may have seen the app automatically installed on your devices throughout the course of the day. The ARC app adds an even more robust communication channel between Government and citizens.

I have spoken this afternoon with the leaders of every affected nation. We are united — not only in our response, but in our resolve. This was an attack on all of us. It will be met by all of us.

In the meantime, I ask just three things of you.

First: for the next 36 hours, stay local, stay safe. Do not drive, unless it is a matter of life or death. This is not a lockdown, but a request. Look after each other. Check on your neighbours. Share what you have.

Second: do not fear. We will restore these systems. We will provide answers. And we will ensure that every family in this country is supported through this period. This period of days, not weeks.

Third: please continue to follow the guidance issued through ARC, the emergency alert system and on all BBC television and radio channels.

I will address you again within 24 hours and there will be detailed updates from my colleagues in the Cabinet and experts from the National Cyber Security Centre during this period.

There are dark days, challenging days, ahead. We face them with our unique British spirit. We face them together.

Good night. And be well.

items.text: PM’s Address to the Nation — Full Transcript

article.title: PM’s Address to the Nation — Full Transcript
article.body:
Five weeks ago, on a Friday night, the lights went out.

For some of us it was the lights in our homes. For all of us it was more than this. Much more. The systems we relied upon to move our money, keep our records safe, that held the invisible architecture of daily life in place — they began to flicker. And then they went dark. And in that darkness, you did something remarkable.

You looked after each other.

I have spent these five weeks visiting communities across this country. I have sat in leisure centres, school gymnasiums and supermarket car parks. I have watched volunteers — strangers, neighbours, teenagers, pensioners — work together for the community and for one another, organising food distribution with nothing more than clipboards and goodwill. I have seen this country at its most bare and its most unified. And I have never been more proud to lead it.

But pride is not a plan. You deserve a plan, and I am here, today, to deliver that plan.

You deserve the truth. You have always deserved the truth. It pains me to say that prior to this egregious assault on our way of life, you have not always been given it. From this day onwards, that changes. That is my vow. And it is the vow of the leaders of every nation that stand together, as one, before you tonight. We will deliver the truth — openly, sincerely, and with integrity.

First, I must be clear about one thing. The system that failed us on the fourteenth of February will not be repaired — it cannot be repaired. Not slowly, not partially. The financial infrastructure that underpinned our economy — the databases, the transaction networks, the ledgers that recorded who owned what and who owed what — sustained damage beyond recovery. The experts we have consulted — and we have consulted every credible expert available — are unanimous.

We cannot go back. But we can, we must, and we will go forwards.

Because something survived.

Resilience. A resilience that lives within each and every one of us. A resilience we built together and that will last forever. The neighbours who checked on each other. The strangers who became friends in a queue. The teenagers who carried shopping for people they’d never met. You did not wait to be told. You did not wait for permission. You acted. We relied upon one another. And that reliance — that trust in each other — is the foundation everything else is built on.

But this is not all that survived.

In 2025, this government — alongside twenty-two partner nations — commissioned a programme. A resilience programme. A digital infrastructure designed not to replace the existing system, but to survive its failure. It was called the Autonomous Resilience Cloud — ARC. Some of you will recognise the name. It has been the backbone of the emergency information service on your phones these past five weeks. It was ARC that kept communication channels open. It was ARC that coordinated the hamper distribution. It was ARC that ensured your hospitals could still identify you and your children’s schools could still find you.

ARC was not a contingency. It was a conviction. A recognition that the systems we had inherited were fragile, centralised, and overdue for replacement. We hoped we would never need it. We were wrong to hope. We were right to build.

And built on the foundation of ARC is something new. Something we believe represents the most significant step forward in the relationship between citizen and state in the modern era.

Her name is AIDA.

AIDA — the Adaptive Intelligence for Domestic Assistance — is your personal recovery assistant. She is not a government database. She is not surveillance. She is a service — designed for us, accountable to us, and available to us all from tonight. AIDA will manage our recovery allocation. She will help us access healthcare, education, housing, employment. She will know what we need because we will tell her, and she will learn. She is built on transparency. Every decision she makes on our behalf is visible to us all. Every recommendation, we can refuse. She works for us. No longer us for them.

She managed the food — no one went hungry. She managed the power, and she kept the lights on.

Now I want to talk to you about what comes next. It impacts what we own and what we owe. This uncertainty has kept us awake these past five weeks.

I am here to tell you: tonight we will all sleep well.

As of eight o’clock this evening, His Majesty’s Treasury — in coordination with the Bank of England and twenty-two partner nations — has enacted a complete jubilee on personal debt. Your mortgage is cancelled. Your credit card balance is zero. Your student loan is cleared. Your overdraft is closed, at zero. This is not a freeze. This is not a deferral. The debt is gone. It does not exist. You owe nothing.

I will say that again, because I know you need to hear it twice.

You owe nothing. To anyone.

The old ledger is gone. The new one starts clean. BritCoin — our new digital allocation — will be credited to every registered household from midnight tonight. Ten thousand BritCoin per adult. Two thousand per child. A monthly allocation follows: fifteen hundred per adult, seven hundred and fifty per child. This is not furlough. This is not a loan. This is not temporary. This is the foundation of our new financial lives, and it begins tonight.

Registration is open now. It takes ninety seconds. You can do it from your phone, or you can visit your local Community Recovery Hub tomorrow morning. The process is simple because we built it to be simple. We have carried enough complexity.

What does registration mean? It means you are choosing to participate in both the National and the Global Recovery Programmes. It means AIDA can see each and every one of us — can allocate to us, can serve us, can protect us. Registration ensures that we can reach you. We can credit you. We can include you in the systems that will, from tonight, begin rebuilding our community, our country, our planet. Registration is not compulsory. But the recovery is real, and it is here, and it is here for all of us. No one should miss out. No one will miss out.

This is not a British project. It is global. This is not financial. It is human. This is not for the few. It is for us all.

Tonight, twenty-three nations are making this same announcement. The same jubilee. The same framework. The same commitment. From Washington to Berlin, from Tokyo to Canberra, from Delhi to São Paulo — the same words, the same promise, the same fresh start. This response was designed in five weeks, but built upon decades of planning, coordination, unity and trust.

The world you wake up to tomorrow will not look the same as the one you lost five weeks ago. It will look better. Not because the crisis was a gift — it was a catastrophe, and we grieve with every family that has suffered. But because the response to that catastrophe has given us permission to do what decades of politics could not: start again.

Tonight we register. Tomorrow we dream.

Our future is now.
